source_text: ἐπιεικεστέροις ἀσφαλές. Γέγραπται γὰρ «Ὁ συμπορευόμενος σοφοῖς, σοφὸς ἔσται· ὁ δὲ συμπορευόμενος ἄφροσι, γνωσθήσεται.» Γράφει δὲ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος· «Ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος πλεονέκτης, ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης, ἢ λοίδορος, ἢ μέθυσος, ἢ ἅρπαξ, τῷ τοιούτῳ μηδὲ συνεσθίειν.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ ἔφης· τὸ γάρ τοι χρῆμά ἐστιν οὐκ ἀσυντελὲς εἰς ὄνησιν. {ΚΥΡ.} Νηκτῶν μὲν δὴ πέρι καὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι ταυτὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς αἰνιγματωδῶς ὁ νόμος. Κατευρύνων δὲ ὥσπερ τῶν παραδειγμάτων ἡμῖν τὴν παράθεσιν, ἐπὶ τὰς πτηνῶν ἀγέλας ἐπιφέρει λέγων· «Καὶ ταῦτα βδελύξεσθε ἀπὸ τῶν πετεινῶν, καὶ οὐ βρωθήσεται· βδέλυγμά ἐστι· τὸν ἀετὸν καὶ τὸν γρύπα, καὶ τὸν ἁλιαίετον, καὶ τὸν γύπα, καὶ τὸν ἰκτῖνον, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ στρουθὸν, καὶ γλαῦκα, καὶ λάρον, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ πάντα κόρακα καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ ἱέρακα καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ νυκτικόρακα, καὶ καταράκτην, καὶ ἴβιν, καὶ πορφυρίωνα, καὶ πελεκᾶνα, καὶ κύκνον, καὶ ἐρωδιὸν, καὶ χαράδριον καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ ἔποπα, καὶ νυκτερίδα, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἑρπετὰ τῶν πετεινῶν, ἃ πορεύεται ἐπὶ τέσσαρα, βδελύγματά ἐστιν ὑμῖν. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα φάγεσθε ἀπὸ τῶν ἑρπετῶν τῶν πετεινῶν, ἃ πορεύεται ἐπὶ τέσσαρα, ἃ ἔχει σκέλη ἀνώτερον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῶν, πηδᾷν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ ταῦτα φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτῶν, τὸν βροῦχον καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ τὸν ἀττάκην καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ ὀφιομάχην καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ τὴν ἀκρίδα καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῇ. Πᾶν ἑρπετὸν ἀπὸ τῶν πετεινῶν, οἷς εἰσι τέσσαρες πόδες, βδελύγματά ἐστιν ὑμῖν, καὶ ἐν τούτοις μιανθήσεσθε. Πᾶς ὁ ἁπτόμενος τῶν θνησιμαίων αὐτῶν, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται ἕως ἑσπέρας.» Ἆρά σοι σαφὴς τῶν εἰρημένων ὁ νοῦς; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἥκιστά γε. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἢ οὐκ αἰσθάνῃ λοιπὸν, ὡς ἐν ἴσῳ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἠθῶν εἶεν ἂν εἰκόνες καὶ τρόπων διαφοραὶ, τὰ ἑκάστου τῶν ὠνομασμένων ἴδια φυσικῶς; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πῶς ἔφης; {ΚΥΡ.} Βούλει λέγωμεν ἀνὰ μέρος, ἕκαστα λεπτῶς διακρίναντες; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀποφάσκει τοίνυν ὁ νόμος τὸν ἀετὸν καὶ τὸν γρύπα, καὶ τὸν ἁλιαίετον, καὶ μέντοι τὸν γύπα· διίπταται γὰρ τὰ τοιάδε ὑψοῦ, καὶ τοῖς ἀνωτάτω λίαν ἐναβρύνεσθαι φιλεῖ, καὶ μισεῖ τὰ κάτω· «Νεοσσοὶ γὰρ,» φησὶ, «γυπὸς τὰ ὑψηλὰ πέτονται.» Τοιουτοσί πως δὲ ὁ ἀλαζὼν καὶ ἐξωφρυωμένος ἄγαν, καὶ ἐπηρμένον ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν νοῦν ἔχων, καὶ τοῦ μὲν ἐπιεικοῦς καὶ μετρίου φρονήματος ὑπερορᾷν εἰθισμένος, ἥκιστά γε ἀγαπῶν τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπάγεσθαι. Συγκαταψέγει δὲ τούτοις τὸν ἰκτῖνα, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, καὶ κόρακα καὶ τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ, δι' ὧν εὖ μάλα σημαίνεται, τό γε ἁρπάζειν εἰδὸς, καὶ δεινὸν εἰς κακουργίαν ἀνθρώπων γένος· καὶ τοῦ μὲν πρώτου τύπος ὁ ἰκτῖνος, θατέρου γε μὴν, ὁ μελάντατος καὶ βαθύς. Σκοτεινοὶ δέ πως καὶ οὐχ ἅπασιν ἐναργεῖς, οἱ δρι
pass_a_gloss: [continuing] ...with the more decent ones it is safe. For it has been written: 'The one walking together with wise men will be wise; but the one walking together with fools will be known.' And Paul also writes: 'If anyone named a brother is a greedy man, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one not even to eat together.' PALLADIUS: You spoke well; for indeed the matter is not without contribution toward benefit. CYRIL: About swimming creatures, then, and those in the waters the law says these things to us in a riddling way. And widening as it were the setting-beside of the examples for us, it brings on to the flocks of birds, saying: 'And these you shall loathe from the birds, and it shall not be eaten; it is an abomination: the eagle and the griffon-vulture, and the sea eagle, and the vulture, and the kite, and the ones like it, and ostrich, and owl, and gull, and the ones like it, and every raven and the ones like it, and hawk and the ones like it, and night raven, and the plunging bird, and ibis, and purple gallinule, and pelican, and swan, and heron, and plover and the ones like it, and hoopoe, and bat, and all the creeping things of the birds which go upon four, they are abominations to you. But these you shall eat from the creeping things of the birds which go upon four: which have legs higher than their feet, to leap with them upon the earth; and these you shall eat from them: the young locust and the ones like it, and the attakes-locust and the ones like it, and the snake-fighter and the ones like it, and the locust and the ones like it. Every creeping thing from the birds to which there are four feet, they are abominations to you, and in these you shall be defiled. Everyone touching their dead bodies shall be unclean until evening.' Is the sense of the things said clear to you? PALLADIUS: Least of all. CYRIL: Or do you not perceive now that, equally with the others, the natural properties of each of the named creatures would be images of characters and differences of ways? PALLADIUS: How did you say? CYRIL: Do you wish we speak part by part, distinguishing each thing finely? PALLADIUS: Very much so. CYRIL: The law therefore refuses the eagle and the griffon-vulture, and the sea eagle, and indeed the vulture; for such birds fly through on high, and they love to pride themselves very much in the highest things, and they hate the things below. 'For the young of a vulture,' it says, 'fly the high places.' Of such a kind somehow is the boaster and the one very haughty with raised brows, and having his mind lifted up in himself, and accustomed to look down on the decent and moderate way of thinking, least of all loving to be led along together with the lowly. And it blames together with these the kite and the ones like it, and raven and the ones like it, through which is signified very well the race of men that knows how to seize and is clever toward evil-doing; and of the first the type is the kite, but of the other the blackest and deep one. And dark somehow and not clear to all are those who are sh[arp — next section].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …who are more upright it is safe. For it is written: ‘He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be known’ (Proverbs 13:20). And Paul too writes: ‘If anyone called a brother is greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a swindler, do not even eat with such a one’ (1 Corinthians 5:11).
Palladius: Well said; for the matter is not without profit.

Cyril: This, then, is what the law tells us in riddles about creatures that swim and live in the waters. Then, widening, as it were, the range of examples it sets before us, it goes on to the flocks of birds, saying: ‘And these you shall abhor among the birds, and they shall not be eaten; they are an abomination: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the sea eagle, the vulture, the kite and its kind, the ostrich, the owl, the gull and its kind, every raven and its kind, the hawk and its kind, the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican, the swan, the heron, the plover and its kind, the hoopoe and the bat (Leviticus 11:13–19). And all winged creeping things that go on all fours are an abomination to you (Leviticus 11:20). But these you shall eat among the winged creeping things that go on all fours: those that have legs above their feet, with which to leap on the ground. These you shall eat of them: the young locust and its kind, the cricket and its kind, the grasshopper and its kind, and the locust and its kind (Leviticus 11:21–22). Every winged creeping thing that has four feet is an abomination to you, and by these you shall be defiled. Whoever touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 11:23–24). Is the meaning of these words clear to you?
Cyril: Do you not perceive by now that, just as with the others, the traits that belong by nature to each of the creatures named would be images of characters and of different ways of life?
Cyril: Shall we take them one at a time, distinguishing each with care?

Cyril: The law, then, rejects the eagle, the bearded vulture, the sea eagle, and the vulture as well. For birds like these fly about on high; they love to pride themselves on the loftiest heights, and they hate what is low. ‘The young of the vulture,’ it says, ‘fly to the heights’ (Job 5:7). Such, in a way, is the boaster, the man of overweening haughtiness, who has his mind lifted up within himself, who is used to looking down on a gentle and moderate frame of mind, and who has no love at all for associating with the lowly (Romans 12:16). Together with these the law also condemns the kite and its kind, and the raven and its kind. By these it signifies very well the kind of people who know how to plunder and are clever at wrongdoing: the kite is a type of the first, and the deep, jet-black raven of the second. For those who are shrewd…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Pass A rewritten 2026-10-23 as a plain English sense gloss of the Greek: the reviewed gloss interleaved Greek phrases with English, and once the Greek tags moved into lemmas[] too little English was left. Meaning unchanged; Pass B not touched.

Section opens mid-sentence (‘but with those who are more upright it is safe’ begins in section 22), so the first paragraph carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label. Proverbs 13:20 follows the LXX (‘will be known’); the Hebrew has ‘will suffer harm’. Cyril’s 1 Corinthians 5:11 omits ‘sexually immoral’ from Paul’s list; the omission is kept. Leviticus 11:13–24 is quoted from the LXX, with Cyril’s own order of birds (ostrich, owl and gull come before the raven) and insects (ophiomaches before akris); citations are placed by verse groups. Bird and insect names follow the LXX terms, whose identities are uncertain: γρύψ (literally ‘griffin’, Hebrew peres) is rendered ‘bearded vulture’ to keep it distinct from γύψ ‘vulture’; στρουθός in Leviticus 11:16 renders the Hebrew for ostrich and is so translated, though the word can mean ‘sparrow’; καταράκτης ‘cormorant’; χαραδριός ‘plover’ (possibly the nocturnal stone curlew, which fits Cyril’s night birds in section 24); βροῦχος, ἀττάκης, ὀφιομάχης (‘snake fighter’) and ἀκρίς are given as young locust, cricket, grasshopper and locust only as distinct English labels. Job 5:7 is the LXX (‘the young of the vulture fly to the heights’); the Hebrew reads ‘as the sparks fly upward’. ‘Associating with the lowly’ alludes to Romans 12:16 (τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι). ‘The raven’ is supplied for ὁ μελάντατος καὶ βαθύς (‘the blackest and deep one’), which refers back to the raven just named; ‘deep’ keeps the hint of hidden cunning taken up in section 24. οἱ δριμεῖς is ‘the shrewd’. The section ends mid-word (δρι|μεῖς); the sentence completes in section 24.
added ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label; trailing ‘…’ at the mid-word break
checked Proverbs 13:20 (LXX ‘will be known’), 1 Corinthians 5:11, Job 5:7 (LXX), Romans 12:16 (συναπαγόμενοι)
checked the Leviticus 11:13–24 quotation bird by bird and insect by insect against LXX; verse groupings 11:13–19, 11:20, 11:21–22, 11:23–24 confirmed (LXX verse divisions match English here)
